reviewed.front: Define electronegativity.
reviewed.back: Ability of an atom to attract the shared electron pair in a covalent bond.
reviewed.assessment: Individual question and model answer checked; not a claim of complete AQA section coverage

reviewed.front: What do δ+ and δ− mean on a polar bond?
reviewed.back: Partial positive and partial negative charges caused by uneven electron sharing.
reviewed.assessment: Individual question and model answer checked; not a claim of complete AQA section coverage

reviewed.front: Why is an H–Cl bond polar?
reviewed.back: Cl is more electronegative and draws the shared electron pair toward itself.
reviewed.assessment: Individual question and model answer checked; not a claim of complete AQA section coverage

reviewed.front: Why is CO₂ overall non-polar despite two polar C=O bonds?
reviewed.back: Its linear, symmetrical bond dipoles cancel.
reviewed.assessment: Individual question and model answer checked; not a claim of complete AQA section coverage

reviewed.front: Why is BF₃ overall non-polar despite polar B–F bonds?
reviewed.back: Three identical bond dipoles cancel in a symmetrical trigonal planar arrangement.
reviewed.assessment: Individual question and model answer checked; not a claim of complete AQA section coverage

reviewed.front: Why is CCl₄ overall non-polar despite polar C–Cl bonds?
reviewed.back: The tetrahedrally arranged bond dipoles cancel.
reviewed.assessment: Individual question and model answer checked; not a claim of complete AQA section coverage

reviewed.front: Why is H₂O polar?
reviewed.back: Its bent geometry means the polar O–H bond dipoles do not cancel.
reviewed.assessment: Individual question and model answer checked; not a claim of complete AQA section coverage

reviewed.front: How can a molecule have polar bonds but no permanent dipole?
reviewed.back: Its geometry may make equal bond dipoles cancel vectorially.

reviewed.front: Which three intermolecular forces are in AQA 3.1.3.7?
reviewed.back: van der Waals' (induced dipole–dipole) forces, permanent dipole–dipole and hydrogen bonding.
reviewed.assessment: Individual question and model answer checked; not a claim of complete AQA section coverage

reviewed.front: Do all atoms and molecules have van der Waals' (induced dipole–dipole) forces?
reviewed.back: Yes: instantaneous fluctuations create temporary induced dipoles.
reviewed.assessment: Individual question and model answer checked; not a claim of complete AQA section coverage

reviewed.front: What causes induced dipole–dipole (van der Waals') attraction?
reviewed.back: Temporary electron-density fluctuations induce dipoles in neighbouring particles.
reviewed.assessment: Individual question and model answer checked; not a claim of complete AQA section coverage

reviewed.front: Why do van der Waals' forces generally increase for larger molecules?
reviewed.back: More electrons and greater polarizability make induced dipoles stronger.
reviewed.assessment: Individual question and model answer checked; not a claim of complete AQA section coverage

reviewed.front: Why can straight-chain molecules boil above more branched isomers?
reviewed.back: Greater surface contact generally strengthens van der Waals' forces.
reviewed.assessment: Individual question and model answer checked; not a claim of complete AQA section coverage

reviewed.front: When do permanent dipole–dipole forces occur?
reviewed.back: Between neighbouring polar molecules with permanent dipoles.
reviewed.assessment: Individual question and model answer checked; not a claim of complete AQA section coverage

reviewed.front: What atoms must H be bonded to for strong usual hydrogen bonding?
reviewed.back: Nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine.
reviewed.assessment: Individual question and model answer checked; not a claim of complete AQA section coverage

reviewed.front: What other feature is essential for intermolecular hydrogen bonding?
reviewed.back: A nearby lone pair on N, O or F acts as an electron-pair acceptor site.
reviewed.assessment: Individual question and model answer checked; not a claim of complete AQA section coverage

reviewed.front: Does HCl form conventional hydrogen bonds between HCl molecules?
reviewed.back: No; usual hydrogen bonding in this syllabus needs H bonded to N, O or F.
reviewed.assessment: Individual question and model answer checked; not a claim of complete AQA section coverage

reviewed.front: Why does water have unusually high boiling point for its mass?
reviewed.back: An extensive hydrogen-bond network needs substantial energy to overcome.
reviewed.assessment: Individual question and model answer checked; not a claim of complete AQA section coverage

reviewed.front: Why do NH₃, H₂O and HF have anomalous boiling points?
reviewed.back: They can form intermolecular hydrogen bonds.
reviewed.assessment: Individual question and model answer checked; not a claim of complete AQA section coverage

reviewed.front: What happens to covalent O–H bonds when water boils?
reviewed.back: They stay intact; intermolecular hydrogen bonds are overcome instead.
reviewed.assessment: Individual question and model answer checked; not a claim of complete AQA section coverage

reviewed.front: Why is ice less dense than liquid water?
reviewed.back: Its hydrogen bonds create an open tetrahedral network with more empty space.
reviewed.assessment: Individual question and model answer checked; not a claim of complete AQA section coverage

reviewed.front: How many hydrogen bonds can one water molecule form in ideal ice?
reviewed.back: Four: two via its O–H hydrogens and two via lone-pair acceptor sites.
reviewed.assessment: Individual question and model answer checked; not a claim of complete AQA section coverage

reviewed.front: Why does I₂ boil at a higher temperature than Cl₂?
reviewed.back: I₂ has more electrons; stronger van der Waals' (induced dipole–dipole) forces.
reviewed.assessment: Individual question and model answer checked; not a claim of complete AQA section coverage

reviewed.front: How should a boiling-point comparison be explained fully?
reviewed.back: Identify the forces, compare their strength and state the energy needed to overcome them.
reviewed.assessment: Individual question and model answer checked; not a claim of complete AQA section coverage

reviewed.front: Are intermolecular forces and covalent bonds the same?
reviewed.back: No: intermolecular forces attract molecules; covalent bonds join atoms within molecules.

reviewed.front: How are double and triple bonds counted in VSEPR?

reviewed.front: What decides a molecule's shape rather than electron geometry?
reviewed.back: Positions of atoms/bonding regions; lone pairs affect angles but are not named as vertices.

reviewed.front: Why are lone-pair repulsions stronger than bond-pair repulsions?
reviewed.back: Lone-pair electron density is closer to the central atom and repels bonding pairs more.

reviewed.front: What electron-domain shape results from three domains?
reviewed.back: Trigonal planar, approximately 120° before lone-pair distortion.

reviewed.front: Three electron domains: 2 bonds and 1 lone pair. Shape?

reviewed.front: Four electron domains: 2 bonds and 2 lone pairs. Shape?
reviewed.back: Bent, around 104.5° in H₂O.

reviewed.front: Four electron domains: 3 bonds and 1 lone pair. Shape?
reviewed.back: Trigonal pyramidal, about 107° in NH₃.

reviewed.front: Four electron domains: 4 bonds and no lone pairs. Shape?
reviewed.back: Tetrahedral, about 109.5°.

reviewed.front: Five electron domains without lone pairs: shape and angles?
reviewed.back: Trigonal bipyramidal: 90°, 120° and 180°.

reviewed.front: Why do lone pairs prefer equatorial sites in a trigonal bipyramid?

reviewed.front: Five domains: 3 bonds, 2 lone pairs. Shape?

reviewed.front: Five domains: 2 bonds, 3 lone pairs. Shape?

reviewed.front: Six domains: 5 bonds and 1 lone pair. Shape?

reviewed.front: Six domains: 4 bonds and 2 lone pairs. Shape?

reviewed.front: Why are H₂O bond angles smaller than those in NH₃?

reviewed.front: What must you count first to predict a molecule's shape?
reviewed.back: Bonding regions and lone pairs around the central atom.

reviewed.front: How do you identify δ+ and δ− in a polar bond?
reviewed.back: More electronegative atom is δ−; the other atom is δ+.

reviewed.front: Are polar bonds sufficient for a molecular permanent dipole?
reviewed.back: No; the bond dipoles must not cancel when the 3D shape is considered.

reviewed.front: Compare the permanent dipoles of CO₂ and SO₂.
reviewed.back: CO₂: none, linear dipoles cancel. SO₂: present, bent dipoles do not cancel.
reviewed.assessment: Individual question and model answer checked; not a claim of complete AQA section coverage

reviewed.front: Why is NH₃ a polar molecule?
reviewed.back: N–H bonds are polar and trigonal pyramidal shape prevents cancellation.

reviewed.front: Why does CHCl₃ have a permanent dipole but CCl₄ does not?
reviewed.back: CHCl₃ is asymmetrical; CCl₄ is symmetrical with cancelling C–Cl dipoles.
reviewed.assessment: Individual question and model answer checked; not a claim of complete AQA section coverage

reviewed.front: Can a non-polar molecule contain polar bonds? Example?
reviewed.back: Yes. In BF₃ the three polar B–F bond dipoles cancel.

reviewed.front: What are the two checks for molecular polarity?
reviewed.back: Check electronegativity differences in bonds, then whether the 3D dipoles cancel.

reviewed.front: How do bond polarities differ from intermolecular forces?
reviewed.back: Bond polarity concerns uneven sharing within a bond; intermolecular forces act between molecules.

reviewed.front: What name does your class use for induced dipole–dipole attractions?
reviewed.back: Van der Waals' forces (induced dipole–dipole attractions).
reviewed.assessment: Individual question and model answer checked; not a claim of complete AQA section coverage

reviewed.front: What causes van der Waals' forces?
reviewed.back: Temporary electron fluctuations make dipoles that induce dipoles in neighbouring particles.

reviewed.front: Do non-polar molecules experience van der Waals' forces?
reviewed.back: Yes; induced dipoles form even without a permanent molecular dipole.

reviewed.front: Why are van der Waals' forces stronger in I₂ than Cl₂?
reviewed.back: I₂ has more electrons and a more easily polarised cloud, making stronger induced dipoles.

reviewed.front: How do stronger van der Waals' forces affect boiling point?
reviewed.back: More energy is needed to separate molecules, so the boiling point increases.

reviewed.front: Why is water's boiling point anomalously high?
reviewed.back: O–H polarity allows H bonds between δ+ H and a lone pair on O of another molecule.

reviewed.front: Why does HF hydrogen bond strongly but HCl not normally?

reviewed.front: What is overcome when iodine boils: I–I bonds or van der Waals' forces?
reviewed.back: Intermolecular van der Waals' forces; I–I covalent bonds stay intact.

reviewed.front: In boiling water, which bonds stay intact?
reviewed.back: The covalent O–H bonds; intermolecular hydrogen bonds are overcome.

reviewed.front: What must be overcome when an ionic solid melts?
reviewed.back: Strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.

reviewed.front: What happens to the strength of induced dipole forces down Group 7?
reviewed.back: They increase down the group.

reviewed.front: When can a molecule with polar bonds still be non-polar?
reviewed.back: When its bond dipoles cancel because of the molecule's shape.

reviewed.front: Why is NH₃'s bond angle smaller than CH₄'s?
reviewed.back: NH₃ has a lone pair; its stronger repulsion reduces the bond angle.

reviewed.front: When a hydrogen-bonded liquid boils, which bonds are overcome?
